new_statements.quote: 2.3. Stress. The stress is word final in nouns, with just a few exceptions following the norm in Persian, in adverbs such as xálɛ ‘very’. Verb forms appear to follow the stress patterns of Mazandarani proper (see Borjian 2005): the stress is on the verbal prefix in the imperative (báxor ‘eat!’) and the subjunctive (báxori ‘that you eat’); penultimate in the present-future (xorémma ‘I eat’); on the final syllable of the past stem (ba-rɛkkí-a ‘he scratched’, da-pấ-a ‘he threw’); and on the nominal component (vấ dakɛta [lit. wind (n.) it-fell] ‘it swelled’, sâzɛ́ bɛzia ‘he swept’). The negation marker (§4.7) always takes the primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Borjian, Habib. 2019. The Caspian Language of Šahmirzād. Journal of the American Oriental Society 139(2): 361-380. doi:10.7817/jameroriesoci.139.2.0361

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nominals carry stress on the word-final syllable (Persian-type system), with a handful of lexical exceptions among adverbs (e.g. initial-stressed xálɛ 'very'). Verbal stress is morphologically assigned as in Mazandarani: on the modal/verbal prefix ba- in imperative and subjunctive, on the penult in the present-future, on the last syllable of the past stem in past forms (person endings unstressed), on the nominal element of compound verbs, and the negative prefix ná- always attracts primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (only 'primary stress' of the negation marker is mentioned, implying other stresses demote, but no secondary-stress rule is given).
new_statements.exceptions: Adverbs such as xálɛ 'very' (non-final, as in Persian); unstressed person endings (Table 5 'unstressed third person ending'); verb forms follow morphological rules rather than final stress; pluperfect júš baze bea vs compound adjective juš-bazé distinguished by stress position (4.10.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation/elicited forms from the author's field notes and earlier transcriptions (Christensen 1935, Žukovskij 1922, Purkarim ms.); nouns vs. verbs treated separately; no phrase-level discussion. Author flags (2.2.2) that more data are needed on stressed vs. unstressed vowel variation.
new_statements.identity_note: Borjian 2019 describes the language of the town of Šahmirzād (Semnan province) = Glottolog shah1253 / ISO srz exactly; he treats it as a Caspian (Tabaroid) language closely related to Mazandarani (maza1291) and notes its verb-stress patterns match 'Mazandarani proper'. Rastorgueva 1999 likewise treats 'Šamerzadi' as a language/dialect very close to Mazanderani. No dialect-internal variation in stress is reported.

Verb forms appear to follow the stress patterns of Mazandarani proper (see Borjian 2005): the stress is on the verbal prefix in the imperative (báxor ‘eat!’) and the subjunctive (báxori ‘that you eat’); penultimate in the present-future (xorémma ‘I eat’); on the final syllable of the past stem (ba-rɛkkí-a ‘he scratched’, da-pấ-a ‘he threw’); and on the nominal component (vấ dakɛta [lit. wind (n.) it-fell] ‘it swelled’, sâzɛ́ bɛzia ‘he swept’). sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Stress' (p. 366): stress is word-final in nouns, with a few Persian-type exceptions in adverbs (xálɛ 'very'); verbs follow Mazandarani patterns: stress on the verbal prefix in imperative and subjunctive, penultimate in present-future, on the final syllable of the past stem, on the nominal component of compound verbs; negation marker always takes primary stress. Also (2.2.2) notes uncertainty whether vowel variation is conditioned by stressed vs. unstressed syllables.
